title: Deep in one: Exodus
for: I want to know Exodus well
subtitle: Twelve sessions through the book of the great rescue, section by section: the bush, the plagues, the Passover, the sea, Sinai, the calf and the glory filling the tent.
intro: This track reads Exodus whole, a section at a sitting. The book moves from slavery to worship. It opens with a family grown into a people and crushed by a frightened king, and it ends with God living among that people in a tent in the desert. Between those two scenes come the story the rest of the Bible keeps retelling: the burning bush, the plagues, the Passover, the sea, the mountain, the commands, the golden calf and the glory.

Each session opens a chapter of the Study Bible with its notes in plain words, and comes back to one question, one thing to do and one verse. Read the chapters the session names before you begin it. Watch for the threads that run on into the New Testament: the lamb, the covenant sealed with blood, the tent where God dwells, the name he proclaims. By the end you should be able to tell a friend what Exodus is about and why Christians cannot read the Gospels without it. Each session ends with a guide for a group.

about: This guide is for anyone leading a small group through Deep in one: Exodus. The group meets twelve times and reads a section of the book each time, from the slave camps of chapter 1 to the glory filling the tabernacle in chapter 40. It suits people who already believe and people who are only curious, because Exodus asks questions everyone asks: whether God sees the oppressed, what freedom is for, and how a holy God can live among people who keep failing him.

Each person reads the chapters and the session before the group meets. The meeting reads the heart of the section aloud and talks it over, using the group guide for that session, which is gathered below in order with the page each session opens and the question it asks.

sections.title: The group
body: Four to ten people is a good size, small enough that everyone speaks. Meet for about seventy-five minutes, once a week, for twelve meetings, and keep the end time you promised. Some sessions cover several chapters, and the plagues and the tabernacle plans are long, so ask people to read ahead and don't try to discuss every scene in the room. A leader doesn't need to be a scholar. A leader needs to have read the chapters and their notes, and to be willing to admit not knowing.

sections.title: The room
body: Sit in a circle round a table if you can, with the text open in front of everyone, in print or on a phone. Exodus was told and retold at Israel's tables, and it is still read aloud at the Passover meal, so ask a good reader to read the central scene aloud at each meeting, and let people take turns. Make it plain at the first meeting that anyone may pass on any question, that what people say about their own lives stays in the room, and that no one has to pray aloud.

sections.title: The order of a meeting
body: About seventy-five minutes, in this order. Keep to the times loosely and to the end time strictly.
steps: Ten minutes: the opening question, once round the circle. Anyone may pass.
Fifteen minutes: one person reads the central scene of the section aloud while the others follow.
Thirty-five minutes: the three questions to talk over, in order. Ask where each answer is in the text.
Five minutes: one person reads the verse to keep, and the group says what it noticed in it.
Five minutes: the prayer prompt, in your own words.
Five minutes: name the next section and the page its session opens, and say when you will meet.

sections.title: When a hard question comes
body: Exodus raises questions the church has argued over for centuries: when the exodus happened and whether it happened as told, how God could harden Pharaoh's heart and still hold him responsible, why the firstborn of Egypt died, and why the law regulated slavery instead of ending it. When the group reaches one, read the note on it together before anyone answers. Where faithful Christians read a passage in more than one way, give each reading its strongest form and don't settle for the group what the church has not settled. If no one knows, write the question down and bring it back the next week.

Some questions are about whether any of it is true, or about how these chapters have been used. Welcome them. The Honest Answers and the context guides on this site take many of them up, and the sessions link several. Treating a question as disloyalty ends the conversation, and Exodus itself is full of people arguing with God, Moses most of all.

sections.title: When someone is hurting
body: Exodus begins with forced labour and murdered children, and its laws speak of servants, injuries and strangers. Someone in the group may carry a story close to these: work that felt like bondage, a lost child, a home where they were not safe, a country they had to flee. When that happens, stop the discussion and listen. Thank the person for saying it, don't explain their suffering for them, and don't hurry them back to the passage. Ask whether they would like the group to go on or to pause, and speak with them on their own afterwards.

Never let a line from Exodus become a reason for someone to stay where they are being harmed. The God of this book hears the cry of the oppressed and comes down to rescue them. If someone says that a partner, an employer, a leader or anyone else is harming them or a child, take it seriously and don't promise to keep it secret.

sections.title: When to point someone to Find Help
body: Point someone to Find Help when what they carry has become too heavy to set down: grief that has taken their sleep or appetite for weeks, fear or guilt that will not let them rest, harm done to them at home, at work or in a church, or any sign that they no longer want to be alive. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn, and its lines for help right now are open day and night. If anyone is in danger now, call your local emergency number. A leader is a friend in that moment, not a counsellor, and the kindest thing is often to stay with the person while they make the first call.

sessions.title: Slavery, and a baby in the Nile
teaching: Exodus opens where Genesis closed, with Jacob's family in Egypt, and with the blessing of creation come true in them: “the Israelites were fruitful and increased rapidly; they multiplied and became exceedingly numerous” (Exodus 1:7). Then comes the sentence that turns the story: “Then a new king, who did not know Joseph, came to power in Egypt” (Exodus 1:8). A people's growth looks like a threat to a frightened king. He tries forced labour, then the midwives, then the river. Every plan fails, and the first to defy him are two women, Shiphrah and Puah, because “The midwives, however, feared God” (Exodus 1:17).

Moses is drawn out of the very river meant to drown him, raised in Pharaoh's house, and named by Pharaoh's daughter. He grows up, kills an Egyptian he sees beating a Hebrew, and runs to Midian, where he marries and keeps sheep for long years. Then the chapter turns from Moses to God, in four verbs: “God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God saw the Israelites and took notice” (Exodus 2:24-25). Hold on to that. The God of the Bible is met here first in a slave camp, listening.

open.label: Exodus 1, passage by passage
open.why: The new king, the forced labour, the midwives and the order to the river, explained in plain words, with what the first hearers would have noticed.

also.label: Exodus's introduction in the Study Bible
also.why: Who wrote Exodus, when the exodus may have happened, how the book is built, and the views on each, set out fairly.

also.label: The exodus in the Bible's story
also.why: Where the rescue from Egypt sits in the whole story of the Bible, from Abraham before it to the land after it.

also.label: Exodus: the whole book
also.why: The whole book in a few short pictures, to see its shape before you read it section by section.

sessions.question: Exodus says God heard, remembered, saw and took notice long before anything changed. What difference does it make to know that God hears before he acts?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 1 and 2 in one sitting. Write down every person in these chapters who defies Pharaoh, and what each of them risked.

verse.text: So God heard their groaning, and He remembered His covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God saw the Israelites and took notice.

care: A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you felt that no one in power noticed what was happening to you or to people you love?
discuss: Pharaoh's fear drives every cruel decision in chapter 1. How does fear make powerful people cruel, then and now?
Two midwives, a mother, a sister and Pharaoh's own daughter all save Moses. Why might Exodus begin its story of rescue with these women?
Moses tries to bring justice with his own hands and has to run. What does that tell us about the difference between zeal and a calling?
group.pray: Pray for people who are enslaved or exploited today, by name where you know them, and give thanks that God hears the cry of the oppressed.

sessions.title: The burning bush and the name
teaching: Moses is keeping someone else's sheep when he sees a bush that burns and isn't burned up. God calls him by name and tells him to take off his sandals, “for the place where you are standing is holy ground” (Exodus 3:5). Then God says what he has seen and heard, and what he means to do: “I have come down to rescue them” (Exodus 3:8). Moses answers with objections, five of them across two chapters. He is nobody. He doesn't know God's name. They won't believe him. He can't speak well. Send someone else. God answers the first with a promise rather than a list of Moses' strengths: “I will surely be with you” (Exodus 3:12).

When Moses asks for a name, God says, “I AM WHO I AM” (Exodus 3:14), and then gives the name that English Bibles print as LORD in small capitals, the four Hebrew letters often written YHWH. It sounds like the Hebrew verb to be. Jewish readers came to honour the name by not saying it aloud, reading Lord in its place. The name tells Moses that God is not defined by Egypt's gods or by Israel's need. He is who he is, and he will be with them. When Jesus said, “before Abraham was born, I am” (John 8:58), his hearers picked up stones.

open.label: Study Exodus 3, step by step
open.why: The guided study walks you through the bush, the call and the name in seven steps, from reading the chapter to praying it.

also.label: The names of God
also.why: What the name given at the bush means, how it is printed in English Bibles, and the other names by which Scripture calls God.

also.label: Who God is
also.why: Short pictures of what the Bible says God is like, to set beside the God who speaks from the bush.

sessions.question: Moses asked who he was, and God answered with who God is. Which of your own objections to God's call would that answer change?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 3 and 4. List Moses' objections in your own words, and beside each write the answer God gives. Notice which answers are about Moses and which are about God.

verse.text: God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM. This is what you are to say to the Israelites: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’”

group.open: Have you ever been asked to do something you were sure you were the wrong person for? What happened?
discuss: God answers Moses' question about himself with a promise of presence. Why is that a better answer than a list of Moses' strengths?
What does the name God gives at the bush tell us about him, and what does it refuse to tell?
Moses is still objecting in chapter 4, and God is angry with him but still sends him. What does that say about how God works with reluctant people?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group facing a task they feel unfit for, and give thanks that God's answer to our weakness is his own presence.

sessions.title: The plagues and Pharaoh's hard heart
teaching: Pharaoh's first answer sets the terms of the whole contest: “Who is the LORD that I should obey His voice and let Israel go?” (Exodus 5:2). The plagues are the reply. Water turns to blood, then come frogs, gnats, flies, the death of livestock, boils, hail, locusts and darkness, and at the last the firstborn. God says what they are for: “I will execute judgment against all the gods of Egypt” (Exodus 12:12). The Nile, the sun and the king himself were honoured as divine in Egypt, and one by one they are shown to have no power to save. The question of chapter 5 gets its answer. Egypt learns who the LORD is.

Then there is Pharaoh's heart. Exodus says it three ways: God will harden it, it was hard, and Pharaoh hardened it himself (Exodus 8:15). Only from the sixth plague does the narrator say plainly that the LORD hardened it. Christians read this in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition, following Paul in Romans 9, hold that God's purpose stands behind Pharaoh's choices without making them any less his own. Many in the Arminian tradition, with many Jewish readers, hold that God confirmed a road Pharaoh had already chosen. Both agree on this much: Pharaoh is never a man who wanted to do right and was stopped.

open.label: Exodus 9, passage by passage
open.why: The plagues on livestock, boils and hail, with the notes that set out how Christians read the hardening of Pharaoh's heart.

also.label: Hard passages of the Bible
also.why: The passages that trouble careful readers most, each with its note, for the questions the plagues and the firstborn raise.

also.label: The gods of the nations
also.why: What the peoples around Israel believed about their gods, so you can hear the plagues as a contest with Egypt's.

also.label: The sovereignty of God
also.why: What Scripture says about God's rule over all things, and how Christians hold it together with human choice.

sessions.question: When have you seen a heart, perhaps your own, grow harder each time relief came and the pressure lifted?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 7 to 11, and mark each place where the text says Pharaoh's heart was hard. Note who the text says hardened it each time, and when that changes.

verse.text: But I have raised you up for this very purpose, that I might display My power to you, and that My name might be proclaimed in all the earth.

care: Behind every one of those Egyptian doors was a mother. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What is something you once refused to change your mind about, even when the evidence kept coming?
discuss: Pharaoh asks who the LORD is. How do the plagues answer him, and why do they answer in that way?
Christians read the hardening of Pharaoh's heart in different ways. What does each reading protect, and what does it find hard to explain?
Pharaoh hardens his heart each time the pressure lifts. What in us makes relief so dangerous to a promise made in trouble?
group.pray: Pray for soft hearts in the group, and for anyone you know who holds power over others, that they would listen to God and to the people they rule.

sessions.title: Passover
teaching: On the last night in Egypt each household kills a lamb, puts its blood on the doorframe, and eats the meal dressed to travel. God says, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13). Then he does something unusual. In the middle of the story he stops to give instructions for remembering it, year after year, so that when children ask what the meal means, parents will tell them (Exodus 12:26-27). Israel's freedom was to be kept at a table. And a mixed multitude went out with them (Exodus 12:38), so from the first night the people of the exodus were never only one bloodline.

Jesus chose the Passover to explain his death. At that meal he took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20). Paul writes, “Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed” (1 Corinthians 5:7), and John notes that none of Jesus' bones were broken, as none of the lamb's could be (John 19:36; Exodus 12:46). Christians differ over what happens at the Lord's Supper, whether Christ is present in the bread and wine, present by the Spirit, or remembered there, and faithful churches hold each view. They agree that the table tells of a rescue paid for with blood.

open.label: Exodus 12, passage by passage
open.why: The lamb, the blood, the unleavened bread and the night of the firstborn, explained in plain words, with care for readers who grieve.

also.label: The Lamb

also.label: Israel's calendar and festivals
also.why: Where Passover and the feast of unleavened bread sit in Israel's year, and how the feasts shaped Jesus' life and death.

also.label: The Lord's Supper and the table
also.why: What the Christian meal takes from the Passover, how the traditions understand it, and what it asks of the people who share it.

sessions.question: Passover was kept by telling the story to children who asked. Who in your life is asking what your faith means, and what would you tell them?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 12, then Luke 22:7-20. Write down three things Jesus' last meal takes from the first Passover, and one thing it changes.

verse.text: The blood on the houses where you are staying will distinguish them; when I see the blood, I will pass over you. No plague will fall on you to destroy you when I strike the land of Egypt.

care: Behind every one of those Egyptian doors was a mother. If you have lost a child, or carry a grief like hers, please do not carry it alone. Speak to someone you trust, a pastor or a grief counsellor, and if the pain ever feels like more than you can bear, reach out today to a crisis line or emergency service. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What meal or tradition in your family carries a story, and who told it to you?
discuss: Why does God stop the story of the rescue to give instructions for remembering it?
Jesus could have explained his death in many ways. Why the Passover, and what does it say about what his death does?
Christians differ about what happens at the Lord's Supper. What do the views share, and how can we hold the differences with charity?
group.pray: Give thanks for the rescue the Passover pointed to, and pray for the children and young people in your lives, that they will ask and be answered well.

sessions.title: Through the sea
teaching: Pharaoh changes his mind and sends his chariots, and Israel is caught between an army and the water. The people panic and wish they had stayed slaves. Moses tells them, “The LORD will fight for you; you need only to be still” (Exodus 14:14). The wind blows all night, the sea opens, Israel crosses on dry ground, and the waters return over the army. The Hebrew name of the sea is yam suph, often rendered the Sea of Reeds, and where the crossing happened is still argued. The text cares less about the map than about what Israel saw: “the people feared the LORD and believed in Him” (Exodus 14:31).

Then they sing. Many scholars count the song of Moses and Miriam in chapter 15 among the oldest poems in the Bible, and it doesn't flinch from what happened: “the horse and rider He has thrown into the sea” (Exodus 15:21). The rescue of the weak meant the defeat of an army, and the song is honest about both. Later writers kept coming back to this crossing. Isaiah pictured God making “a road in the depths of the sea for the redeemed to cross over” (Isaiah 51:10), and Paul said the fathers “were all baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2).

open.label: Exodus 14, passage by passage
open.why: The trap by the sea, the wind in the night and the crossing, explained in plain words, with the views on where it happened.

also.label: The Exodus
also.why: The story of the rescue from Egypt in short pictures, from the plagues to the far shore of the sea.

also.label: The Bible atlas
also.why: The places of Exodus on the map, Egypt, the sea, the wilderness and the mountain, with the routes scholars propose.

sessions.question: Israel was told to be still while God fought for them. Where are you trying to win a fight that is not yours to win?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 14 and 15. Then read Isaiah 43:16-19, and write down what Isaiah expects God to do again, and what will be new.

verse.text: The LORD is my strength and my song, and He has become my salvation. He is my God, and I will praise Him, my father’s God, and I will exalt Him.

care: If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you been caught with no way forward and no way back?
discuss: The people want to go back to Egypt the moment the chariots appear. Why does slavery look safe when freedom gets hard?
The song celebrates the army's defeat. How should we read a song of victory that includes the drowning of soldiers?
Paul calls the crossing a kind of baptism. What does that suggest about what baptism means for a Christian?
group.pray: Pray for anyone in the group who is caught between two impossible things, and give thanks for the God who makes a way through the sea.

sessions.title: Manna, water and Amalek
teaching: Three days after the song they are thirsty, and within weeks they're hungry and saying Egypt was better. God answers the complaint with bread: “I will rain down bread from heaven for you” (Exodus 16:4). Each morning there is enough for that day, and what is hoarded rots. On the sixth day there is twice as much, so that the seventh can be a rest, and here the word Sabbath appears in the Bible for the first time (Exodus 16:23). The wilderness is a school, and its first lesson is daily dependence. Jesus taught his disciples to ask for daily bread, and he called himself “the bread of life” (John 6:35).

At Massah the people ask, “Is the LORD among us or not?” (Exodus 17:7), and water comes from a rock. Amalek attacks, and Israel wins while Aaron and Hur hold up Moses' tired arms. Then Moses' father-in-law Jethro, a priest of Midian, watches him judge the people from morning to evening and tells him, “You cannot handle it alone” (Exodus 18:18). Wisdom about leadership comes from an outsider, and Moses listens. A people who can't yet trust God for bread are also learning to share one another's weight.

open.label: Exodus 16, passage by passage
open.why: The grumbling, the quail, the manna and the first Sabbath, explained in plain words, with how Jesus took up the bread from heaven.

also.label: How to keep a Sabbath
also.why: Plain steps for a weekly day of rest, the gift first given to a people learning to trust God for bread.

also.label: Rest and the Sabbath
also.why: What Scripture and the long memory of the church say about rest, and why it is a matter of trust and not only of health.

sessions.question: Manna could not be stored up. What are you trying to store up so that you won't need to trust God tomorrow?
sessions.do: This week, before each meal, stop and name where the food came from and who worked for it. Then read Exodus 16 and notice what happens to the bread that is hoarded.

verse.text: When they measured it by the omer, he who gathered much had no excess, and he who gathered little had no shortfall. Each one gathered as much as he needed to eat.

group.open: What do you find hardest to trust God for one day at a time?
discuss: Why do you think God gave bread one day at a time instead of a year's supply?
The people ask whether the LORD is among them or not, after the sea and the manna. Why does memory fail so quickly?
Jethro tells Moses he cannot carry the people alone. Where are you carrying something that should be shared?
group.pray: Pray plainly for the group's daily needs, and for anyone carrying a load alone, that they would let others help them bear it.

sessions.title: Sinai and the covenant
teaching: Three months after leaving Egypt, Israel camps at the foot of the mountain, and before God gives a single command he reminds them what he has already done: “I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself” (Exodus 19:4). The order matters. Israel isn't rescued because it kept the law. It is given the law because it has been rescued. Rescue comes first, then the covenant, then the commands, which describe how a freed people lives with the God who freed it. Grace before law wasn't invented by the New Testament and pressed back onto the Old. It is the shape of Exodus itself.

God then names their calling: “you will be My treasured possession out of all the nations—for the whole earth is Mine. And unto Me you shall be a kingdom of priests and a holy nation” (Exodus 19:5-6). Israel is chosen for the sake of the whole earth, to stand between God and the nations as priests stand between God and a people. Peter gives the same words to the church, “a royal priesthood, a holy nation” (1 Peter 2:9). Then comes the third day: thunder, cloud, a trumpet, smoke, and a mountain no one may touch. The holy God has come near, and nearness to him is not safe.

open.label: Exodus 19, passage by passage
open.why: The eagles' wings, the calling to be a kingdom of priests and the mountain wrapped in smoke, explained in plain words.

also.label: Covenant and treaty
also.why: How covenants between great kings and lesser ones worked in the ancient world, and what that shows about the covenant made at Sinai.

also.label: Covenant
also.why: Short pictures of God's covenants through the Bible, from Noah and Abraham to Sinai, David and the new covenant.

also.label: Holiness
also.why: What Scripture means when it calls God holy, and what it means for a people to be made holy by him.

sessions.question: Israel was rescued before it was given any command. How would your obedience change if you believed that order was true for you?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 19 slowly. Write down every word God says about what he has done, and every word about what Israel is to be, in two columns.

verse.text: You have seen for yourselves what I did to Egypt, and how I carried you on eagles’ wings and brought you to Myself.

group.open: Have you ever been given a gift before you had done anything to deserve it? How did it change you?
discuss: Why does God remind Israel of the eagles' wings before giving any command?
Israel is a kingdom of priests for the sake of the whole earth. What would it look like for a church to take that calling seriously?
The mountain is both near and not safe to touch. How do we hold God's nearness and his holiness together?
group.pray: Give thanks for what God has done before he asks anything of us, and pray for the church to be a priestly people for its neighbours.

sessions.title: The Ten Commandments
teaching: The Ten Commandments begin with a sentence that isn't a command at all: “I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery” (Exodus 20:2). Every command that follows is spoken by a God who has already freed the people he speaks to. The commands describe the life of people who no longer belong to Pharaoh: no other gods, no images, no misuse of his name, a day of rest, honour for parents, and then the protection of a neighbour's life, marriage, property and good name. Jesus summed up the law in two commands, love for God and love for neighbour (Mark 12:29-31), and the ten fall into those two.

Jews and Christians number the ten differently. Jewish tradition counts the opening sentence as the first word. Catholics and Lutherans, following Augustine, join the commands about other gods and images and divide the last. The Orthodox and Reformed count them as most Protestants learn them. The Hebrew calls them the ten words (Exodus 34:28). Notice the Sabbath too. Exodus grounds it in creation, while Deuteronomy grounds it in the rescue: “Remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt” (Deuteronomy 5:15). A day of rest was a weekly sign that no one in Israel was a slave anymore, not even the servants and the animals.

open.label: Study Exodus 20, step by step
open.why: The guided study walks you through the ten words in seven steps, from noticing what the text says to living it this week.

also.label: The law of God
also.why: What the law was for in Israel, how Jesus fulfilled it, and how the Christian traditions understand its place for believers today.

also.label: How to read the law
also.why: How the law books of the Bible work, the kinds of law in them, and how to read them without either skipping or misusing them.

sessions.question: If the commandments describe the life of a freed people, which one shows you most clearly where you are still living like a slave?
sessions.do: Write out the Ten Commandments from Exodus 20 in your own words. Beside each, write who or what it protects.

verse.text: I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. You shall have no other gods before Me.

group.open: What rule from your childhood did you only understand once you were older?
discuss: Why does it matter that the commandments start with what God has done rather than with what Israel must do?
Jesus summed up the law as love for God and love for neighbour. How do the ten fall into those two?
The Sabbath protected servants, foreigners and animals as well as Israelites. What would a day of rest that protected others look like for us?
group.pray: Pray through the commandments slowly as a group, giving thanks for the freedom each one protects and naming quietly where each one finds you.

sessions.title: The book of the covenant, in its world
teaching: After the ten come three chapters of case law: what happens when an ox gores, when a fire spreads, when a loan goes bad. Modern readers often skip them, but they were given to judges in a real ancient society, and they read best beside the other law codes of that world, such as the laws of Hammurabi of Babylon. Set side by side, Exodus shares much with its neighbours and differs in telling ways. Eye for eye (Exodus 21:24) was a limit on revenge given to courts, and it applied to everyone alike, where Hammurabi's laws let a man pay silver for the eye of a commoner or a slave.

These chapters also regulate slavery, and some lines are hard. One calls a servant the owner's property (Exodus 21:21). Critics fairly ask why God's law regulated the institution instead of abolishing it, and Christians owe them an honest answer, not a quick one; the pages linked here take the question at its strongest. What runs through these laws is a memory: “Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners” (Exodus 23:9). The covenant is then sealed with blood, and Moses says, “This is the blood of the covenant” (Exodus 24:8), words Jesus took up at his last supper (Mark 14:24).

open.label: Exodus 21, passage by passage
open.why: The laws on servants and injuries, read in their own world and compared with the other law codes of the ancient Near East.

also.label: The Torah and the law codes
also.why: Israel's law beside the law codes of Mesopotamia, what they share and where the Torah breaks from them.

also.label: Why didn't the Bible just ban slavery?
also.why: The hardest question these chapters raise, taken at its strongest, and what Christians have and have not been able to say in answer.

also.label: How to hold justice and mercy together
also.why: Practical steps for living out a law that protects the stranger, the widow and the poor without losing mercy.

sessions.question: Israel's laws for strangers rested on the memory of being strangers. What memory of your own should shape how you treat people with less power?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 22:21 to 23:9. List every group of vulnerable people these laws protect, and the reason given for protecting each.

verse.text: Do not oppress a foreign resident, since you yourselves know how it feels to be foreigners; for you were foreigners in the land of Egypt.

care: A word for anyone who is being held, owned or forced to work today. It is not your fault. You are not the property of the people who hold you. If you can, please tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
If you are being hurt, at home, at work or in a church, tell someone you trust and get help. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: What law or rule do you think shows most clearly what a society values?
discuss: Eye for eye sounds harsh to us. What changes when we learn it was a limit given to judges?
Why do you think God's law regulated slavery in Israel rather than banning it outright, and what do you make of the answers Christians have given?
Jesus used the words of Exodus 24:8 at his last supper. What does it mean that his covenant is also sealed with blood?
group.pray: Pray for foreigners, widows, orphans and the poor in your town, by name where you can, and ask how the group might protect them.

sessions.title: The tabernacle plans
teaching: Seven chapters now give the plans for a tent: its curtains and frames, the ark and its cover, the lampstand, the altar, the priests' clothes. It's easy to lose patience here, so ask why the detail matters. The answer is in one verse: “they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them” (Exodus 25:8). The God who came down to rescue now means to stay. And the tent is a small garden. Cherubim, who guarded the way to the tree of life after Eden (Genesis 3:24), are woven into its curtains, and the lampstand is shaped like a flowering tree. Many readers have seen in it a way back to the place where God walked with people.

The plans close with Bezalel, a craftsman God fills “with the Spirit of God, with skill, ability, and knowledge in all kinds of craftsmanship” (Exodus 31:3), so even the work of hands is a gift of the Spirit. The rest of the Bible keeps returning to this tent. John writes, “The Word became flesh and made His dwelling among us” (John 1:14), and the Greek verb means he pitched his tent. Hebrews calls Christ the high priest of “the greater and more perfect tabernacle that is not made by hands” (Hebrews 9:11). The tent was never the point. God with his people was.

open.label: Exodus 25, passage by passage
open.why: The offering for the sanctuary, the ark, the table and the lampstand, explained in plain words, with what each meant to Israel.

also.label: God with his people
also.why: Short pictures of God's presence through the whole Bible, from the garden to the tabernacle, the temple, Jesus and the new creation.

also.label: The temple
also.why: What the tabernacle and the temple meant, and how the New Testament finds them fulfilled in Jesus and his people.

also.label: Offerings and purity
also.why: What the offerings and the rules of clean and unclean were for, so the tabernacle chapters make sense as worship.

sessions.question: God gave his people a tent so he could live among them. What would change in an ordinary week if you believed he means to dwell with you?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 25, then John 1:1-18. Write down every word or picture from the tabernacle that you can find in John's opening.

verse.text: And they are to make a sanctuary for Me, so that I may dwell among them.

group.open: Where do you feel most at home, and what makes it so?
discuss: Why do you think Exodus gives so much space to the plans for the tabernacle?
What does the picture of the tent as a small Eden suggest about what God has wanted from the beginning?
John says the Word pitched his tent among us. How does reading Exodus change what you hear in John 1:14?
group.pray: Give thanks that God chose to live among his people, and pray for the group's homes, work and gatherings to be places where he is welcome.

sessions.title: The golden calf
teaching: While Moses is on the mountain receiving the plans for God's dwelling, the people below make their own. Moses is late, and they say to Aaron, “Come, make us gods who will go before us” (Exodus 32:1). Aaron takes their gold, shapes a calf, and announces “a feast to the LORD” (Exodus 32:5). They don't think they have abandoned the God who brought them out of Egypt. They have remade him into something they can see, carry and manage. That is the heart of idolatry, then and now, and it happens most easily when God seems slow.

God tells Moses he will destroy the people and begin again with him, and Moses refuses the offer. He pleads, reminds God of his promises to Abraham, and prays that God would forgive their sin, and the sentence breaks off unfinished. Then he offers himself: “please blot me out of the book that You have written” (Exodus 32:32). In chapter 33 he asks for the one thing that matters. If God's presence doesn't go with them, “do not lead us up from here” (Exodus 33:15). A promised land without God would be only land.

open.label: Exodus 32, passage by passage
open.why: The calf, Aaron's excuse, the broken tablets and Moses' prayer, explained in plain words, with what the book of life means.

also.label: Idolatry
also.why: What Scripture means by idolatry, why it is the root of other sins, and the shapes it takes among believers now.

also.label: How to confess sin and walk in repentance
also.why: Plain steps for confession, for anyone who sees their own calf in this chapter and wants to turn back.

sessions.question: The calf was a god the people could manage. What have you shaped God into so that he would be easier to live with?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 32 and 33. Underline every time Moses speaks to God, and notice what he appeals to: the people's goodness, or God's own name and promises.

verse.text: And the LORD answered, “My Presence will go with you, and I will give you rest.”

care: Sometimes guilt that will not lift needs more than a Bible verse. It can be part of anxiety, depression or a habit of the mind that keeps returning to the same fear. That is not a failure of faith. Talk with a pastor or a friend you trust. If the fear will not let you rest, a counsellor or a doctor can help too, and the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

group.open: When have you found waiting harder than anything else you were asked to do?
discuss: Aaron calls the calf's festival a feast to the LORD. Why is remaking the true God more dangerous than turning to a different one?
Moses appeals to God's promises, not the people's goodness. What does that teach us about how to pray for people who have failed?
Moses would rather stay in the desert with God than enter the land without him. What would it mean for us to want God's presence more than his gifts?
group.pray: Pray for one another as Moses prayed for Israel, appealing to God's own mercy and promises, and confess quietly where we have made God smaller than he is.

sessions.title: The glory passes by, and fills the tent
teaching: Moses asks to see God's glory, and God hides him in a cleft of the rock and passes by, proclaiming his own name: “The LORD, the LORD God, is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness” (Exodus 34:6). This is the Bible's own summary of who God is, and it is echoed again and again, by Moses in Numbers, by the psalmists, by Joel, and by Jonah in a complaint. It goes on to say that he forgives iniquity and will not leave the guilty unpunished. Mercy and justice are both in his name, and Exodus doesn't let you keep one without the other.

Moses comes down with his face shining, and the last chapters build what was planned, almost word for word, until “the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle” (Exodus 40:34). Even Moses can't go in. The book that began with a groan in a slave camp ends with God living in the middle of his people. But they are still in the desert, a long way from the land, and the next books show how hard it is to live near a holy God. Exodus closes on a cloud that leads them, and on a question: whether a people so quick to make a calf can live with him. The next track in this program takes you into the Psalms, where his people learned to pray that question aloud.

open.label: Exodus 34, passage by passage
open.why: The new tablets, the name proclaimed on the mountain and Moses' shining face, explained in plain words, with where the name is echoed.

also.label: Follow a verse through the Bible
also.why: Start from Exodus 34:6 and follow the places across the Bible that take up the name God proclaimed to Moses.

also.label: Exodus 40, passage by passage
also.why: The tabernacle set up, the cloud covering it and the glory filling it, the end of the book explained in plain words.

also.label: Deep in one: the Psalms

sessions.question: Exodus ends with God present and the people still in the wilderness. What does it mean to you that God's presence comes before the promised land?
sessions.do: Read Exodus 34:1-10 and 40:34-38. Then go back to Exodus 2:23-25 and write down how the book has answered the groan it began with, and what it leaves still waiting.

group.open: Which of these twelve sessions will stay with you longest, and why?
discuss: God's name in Exodus 34 holds mercy and justice together. Why do we find it so hard to keep both?
The glory fills the tent, yet Moses cannot enter. What does that tell us about God's nearness and his holiness?
Christians say Jesus is where God's glory now dwells among us. How has Exodus changed the way you will read the Gospels?
group.pray: Give thanks by name for each person in the group, and ask that the God who is compassionate and gracious would go with each of you into the week ahead.
